questions.q: What is an enzyme's active site?

distractors: The region of an enzyme where a regulatory molecule binds, away from the substrate.
The region of the cell where enzymes are produced by ribosomes.
The region of an enzyme's interior that is hidden from the substrate and stabilizes its folded shape.
The region on a substrate that binds to an enzyme.
The region of an enzyme that is altered permanently after each reaction.
The region of a substrate where the products are released.

questions.q: What is a binding site?
questions.answer: The site on a substrate or reactant that binds to an enzyme.
distractors: The region of an enzyme that is altered permanently when a substrate binds.
The location in the nucleus where mRNA is made from DNA.
The region of a hormone where it is synthesized by the cell.
The region of an enzyme's surface where substrates bind for a chemical reaction.
The region of a polymer where hydrolysis occurs.
The region of a cell membrane where hormones attach.

questions.q: How do enzymes generally function, in terms of substrates and products?
questions.answer: Reactants attach to the enzyme's active site; the substrates are converted into a product, which then separates and diffuses away, freeing the enzyme to work again.
distractors: The enzyme adds its own atoms to the substrates and is used up as part of the product.
Substrates are broken apart outside the enzyme, and the pieces then bind to the active site as inactive fragments.
The enzyme binds the substrate and converts it into a product, but must then be replaced by a newly synthesized enzyme molecule.
Reactants permanently bond to the enzyme, forming a single fused molecule.
The enzyme is consumed and destroyed after each reaction it catalyzes.
Products bind to the enzyme's active site before being converted back into reactants.

questions.q: What is a biochemical pathway?
questions.answer: A sequence of chemical reactions in which the product of one reaction becomes the substrate of the next.
distractors: A channel in the cell membrane through which substrates enter the cell.
A single enzyme that binds many different substrates in turn.
A group of reactions that occur in different cells with no shared molecules.
A single reaction that produces many unrelated products at once.
A random series of reactions with no fixed order.
A pathway in which each reaction runs independently of the others' products.

questions.q: What effect can higher temperatures have on an enzyme?
questions.answer: They can weaken the enzyme's bonds, causing it to lose its proper shape and denature.
distractors: They lower the activation energy by enlarging the enzyme's active site.
They make the enzyme bind its substrate more tightly by strengthening its hydrogen bonds.
They change the enzyme's amino acid sequence so that it catalyzes a different reaction.
They always increase the enzyme's reaction rate with no upper limit.
They permanently strengthen the enzyme's active site.
They have no effect on enzyme shape or function.

questions.q: What is a repressor?
questions.answer: A protein that regulates transcription of mRNA from DNA by binding to the operator, preventing RNA polymerase from attaching to the promoter.
distractors: A protein that binds mRNA to prevent it from attaching to the ribosome.
An enzyme that removes introns from mRNA after transcription.
A small molecule that binds to the promoter and makes DNA replicate faster.
A protein that binds to DNA to make it more accessible for transcription.
A protein that increases the rate of translation at the ribosome.
A protein that permanently deletes a gene from the DNA sequence.

questions.q: What is an activator, in the context of gene regulation?
questions.answer: A regulatory protein that binds to DNA, making it more accessible for transcription.
distractors: A regulatory protein that binds to the ribosome to speed up the translation of mRNA.
A protein that unwinds the DNA double helix at the replication fork.
A protein that cuts DNA at the promoter so genes can be transcribed.
A regulatory protein that binds to the operator to block RNA polymerase.
A protein that breaks down mRNA after it is transcribed.
A protein that directly synthesizes new DNA strands.

questions.q: What is feedback inhibition?
questions.answer: A regulatory mechanism in which a biochemical pathway is regulated by the amount of product that the pathway produces.
distractors: A regulatory mechanism in which the product activates the first enzyme in the pathway to speed up further production.
A regulatory mechanism in which the substrate at the start of a pathway shuts off the last enzyme.
A regulatory mechanism in which enzymes are made more slowly when the cell is deprived of oxygen.
A regulatory mechanism in which a pathway speeds up as more substrate becomes available.
A regulatory mechanism in which enzymes are permanently deactivated after one use.
A regulatory mechanism that only functions in the absence of oxygen.

questions.q: What is adenosine triphosphate (ATP)?
questions.answer: A molecule composed of ribose, adenine, and a triphosphate group; the chief energy currency of cells, formed from ADP and phosphate using energy from photosynthesis or food, and used to drive endergonic reactions.
distractors: A molecule composed of glucose and three phosphate groups; the main long-term energy storage molecule of animal cells.
A molecule composed of ribose, guanine, and a monophosphate group; the chief carrier of electrons in cellular respiration.
A molecule composed of adenine, glycerol, and three fatty acids; the main structural component of the cell membrane.
A molecule composed of deoxyribose, thymine, and a diphosphate group used to store genetic information.
A molecule composed of glycerol and three fatty acid chains used for long-term energy storage.
A molecule composed of a 6-carbon sugar and two phosphate groups used only during fermentation.

questions.q: What is cellular respiration?
questions.answer: The process by which energy in a glucose molecule is released through oxidation, as hydrogen atoms are lost by glucose and gained by oxygen.
distractors: The process by which animals take in oxygen from the air and release CO2 through lungs or gills.
The process by which cells build large molecules from small ones, using energy from ATP.
The process by which ATP is broken down to release energy, without involving glucose or oxygen.
The process by which plants capture light energy to build glucose from CO2 and water.
The process by which polymers are broken down into monomers using water.
The process by which proteins are folded into their final three-dimensional shape.

questions.q: What is a redox reaction?
questions.answer: A chemical process in which electrons move from one substrate to another.
distractors: A chemical process in which two monomers are joined and a molecule of water is released.
A chemical process in which atoms are rearranged without any change in energy.
A chemical process in which one molecule transfers its phosphate group to another.
A chemical process in which water is added to break a polymer apart.
A chemical process in which a substrate is permanently destroyed without forming a product.
A chemical process in which only protons, never electrons, are exchanged.

questions.q: What happens to an atom during oxidation, and what does it occur simultaneously with?
questions.answer: An electron is lost from one atom to another; oxidation occurs simultaneously with reduction.
distractors: An electron is lost from one atom to another; oxidation occurs simultaneously with phosphorylation.
A proton is gained by one atom from another; oxidation occurs simultaneously with reduction.
An electron is gained by one atom from another; oxidation occurs simultaneously with hydrolysis.
An electron is gained by one atom from another; oxidation occurs simultaneously with reduction.
A proton is lost from one atom to another; oxidation occurs simultaneously with hydrolysis.
An electron is lost from one atom to another; oxidation occurs simultaneously with dehydration.

questions.q: What is an oxidation-reduction (redox) reaction pair?
questions.answer: A pair of reactions in living systems where electrons lost from one atom are gained by another atom.
distractors: A pair of reactions in which one substrate is split into two identical halves.
A pair of reactions where a phosphate group is removed from one molecule and added to another.
A pair of reactions in which electrons are gained by both atoms at the same time.
A pair of reactions where protons, not electrons, are exchanged between atoms.
A single reaction where an atom simultaneously loses and gains the same electron.
A pair of reactions that only occur in the absence of enzymes.

questions.q: What happens during Stage 1 of cellular respiration?
questions.answer: Coupled reactions make ATP; this stage is better known as glycolysis.
distractors: Acetyl-CoA is oxidized to CO2 in the matrix, releasing NADH, FADH2, and one ATP per turn.
Protons flow back through ATP synthase, driving the phosphorylation of ADP.
Pyruvate is reduced to lactic acid or ethanol to regenerate NAD+.
Oxygen is used in the mitochondrion to make NADH and FADH2.
Electrons are passed down a chain of membrane proteins to pump protons.
Pyruvate is converted into acetyl-CoA and CO2.

questions.q: What happens during Stage 2 of cellular respiration?
questions.answer: An aerobic stage, taking place in the mitochondrion, that uses NADH and FADH2.
distractors: A stage that occurs in the chloroplast, using light energy to make NADPH.
A stage in which pyruvate is exported from the cell and converted back to glucose.
A stage that takes place on the ribosome, using NADH to synthesize proteins.
An anaerobic stage, taking place in the cytoplasm, better known as glycolysis.
A stage that occurs only in the absence of oxygen, producing lactic acid.
A stage that occurs in the nucleus, producing new DNA strands.

questions.q: What is substrate-level phosphorylation?
questions.answer: Generation of ATP by coupling its synthesis to a strongly exergonic (energy-yielding) reaction.
distractors: Generation of ATP by ATP synthase as protons flow down a gradient across a membrane.
Generation of ATP by transferring a phosphate group from NADH to ADP.
Generation of ATP by reducing oxygen to water at the end of a chain of proteins.
Generation of ATP using only the electron transport chain and a proton gradient.
Generation of ATP by directly absorbing light energy.
Generation of ATP by breaking down ATP itself into ADP and phosphate.

questions.q: What is Acetyl-CoA?
questions.answer: The product of the transition between glycolysis and the Krebs cycle, formed when pyruvate is oxidized by NAD+, also producing CO2 and NADH.
distractors: The 4-carbon sugar that combines with a 2-carbon fragment at the start of the Krebs cycle.
The 3-carbon molecule produced when glucose is split in glycolysis.
The electron carrier that delivers electrons from the Krebs cycle to the electron transport chain.
The final product of the Krebs cycle, formed when citrate is broken down completely.
The first product of glycolysis, formed directly from glucose.
The molecule that directly accepts electrons at the end of the electron transport chain.

questions.q: What is the Krebs cycle, and by what other names is it known?
questions.answer: Also called the citric acid cycle or the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle; it works in three phases and is named after the scientist who discovered it.
distractors: Also called the Calvin cycle; it takes place in the stroma of the chloroplast and fixes carbon into sugar.
Also called oxidative phosphorylation; it takes place in the inner mitochondrial membrane and makes most of the cell's ATP.
Also called the Cori cycle; it recycles lactate from muscle to the liver.
Also called glycolysis; it works in a single phase and takes place in the cytoplasm.
Also called the electron transport chain; it works in four phases and takes place in the intermembrane space.
Also called fermentation; it works in two phases and requires no enzymes.

questions.q: What happens in Phase 1 of the Krebs cycle?
questions.answer: The 2-carbon acetyl-CoA fragment produced by pyruvate attaches to a 4-carbon sugar, forming a 6-carbon sugar.
distractors: The 6-carbon sugar is split into two 3-carbon molecules, generating two ATP.
A 4-carbon sugar is converted into pyruvate, and NADH is used to make lactic acid.
Protons flow through ATP synthase, phosphorylating ADP.
Two carbon atoms are removed as CO2, and one ATP molecule is made.
Two carbon atoms are expelled as CO2, leaving only a 4-carbon sugar behind.
Electrons are passed to oxygen to form water.

questions.q: What happens in Phase 2 of the Krebs cycle?
questions.answer: Two carbons are quickly removed as CO2, their electrons donate to NAD+, and one ATP molecule is made.
distractors: Acetyl-CoA is formed from pyruvate as CO2 is released.
Protons are pumped into the intermembrane space by membrane protein complexes.
The 4-carbon sugar is regenerated and can accept another 2-carbon acetyl fragment.
A 2-carbon acetyl-CoA fragment attaches to a 4-carbon sugar to form a 6-carbon sugar.
Two carbon atoms are expelled as CO2, leaving only a 4-carbon sugar, with more energetic electrons captured as NADH or FADH2.
Oxygen accepts electrons to form water at the end of the chain.

questions.q: What happens in Phase 3 of the Krebs cycle?
questions.answer: Two more carbon atoms are expelled as CO2, and more energetic electrons are extracted and carried away as NADH or FADH2, leaving only the 4-carbon sugar.
distractors: Glucose is oxidized to two pyruvate molecules with a net gain of two ATP.
Oxygen is reduced to water as electrons reach the end of a membrane chain.
Lactic acid is formed to regenerate NAD+ when oxygen is absent.
A 2-carbon acetyl-CoA fragment attaches to a 4-carbon sugar to form a 6-carbon sugar.
Two carbons are quickly removed as CO2 and one ATP molecule is made.
Pyruvate is converted into acetyl-CoA for the first time.

questions.q: What is the intermembrane space of a mitochondrion?
questions.answer: The outer compartment of a mitochondrion that lies between its two membranes.
distractors: The folded inner membrane of the mitochondrion that bears the electron transport chain.
The space between the two membranes of the nuclear envelope.
The fluid inside a chloroplast that surrounds the thylakoids.
The innermost compartment of a mitochondrion, enclosed by the inner membrane.
The fluid-filled space inside the nucleus.
The space between the cell membrane and the cell wall.

questions.q: What is the electron transport chain?
questions.answer: A series of membrane-associated protein complexes embedded in the inner mitochondrial membrane that uses electrons from glucose oxidation to drive proton-pumping channels.
distractors: A series of enzymes in the mitochondrial matrix that oxidize acetyl-CoA to CO2.
A single protein in the outer mitochondrial membrane that pumps ATP out of the mitochondrion.
A series of reactions in the cytoplasm that convert pyruvate to ethanol or lactic acid.
A series of enzymes in the cytoplasm that break glucose into pyruvate.
A single membrane channel that directly converts glucose into ATP without electrons.
A series of reactions in the Krebs cycle that produce CO2 as the final product.

questions.q: What is fermentation, in terms of its final electron acceptor?
questions.answer: A catabolic process in which the final electron acceptor is an organic molecule (such as pyruvate), not oxygen.
distractors: A catabolic process in which the final electron acceptor is inorganic, such as sulfate or nitrate, rather than oxygen.
A process in which oxygen is reduced to water at the end of the electron transport chain.
A process in which glucose is oxidized completely to CO2 using the Krebs cycle.
A catabolic process in which the final electron acceptor is always oxygen.
An anabolic process that builds glucose from CO2 and water using light energy.
A process that occurs exclusively inside the mitochondrion.
